These formations crop out on both limbs of the salient and earlier, but less definitive paleomagnetic studies on these units indicate that early acquired magnetizations can be recovered. Oriented samples were obtained from nine sites on the southern limb of the salient and eight sites from the northern limb in the Bloomsburg. The natural remanent magnetizations are multivectorial, dominated by a component (B) with a distributed spectrum of unblocking temperatures ranging up to 670øC, and a component (C) with a higher and very discrete distribution of unblocking temperatures. In contrast, samples from the southern sites tend to have a reversed polarity C component, with an appreciable to dominant contribution from the B component (Figure 2c) as previously observed by Roy et al. Least squares fits to the linear demagnetization trajectories for the B and C components in each sample were made by principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980]. Only site K did not yield a reliable B component sample direction and except for single determinations at sites Q and R, all other sites yielded three to seven sample estimates for both the B and C components (Tables 1 and 2). The site mean directions for the B component are southerly and shallow from both the northern and southern areas (Figure 3a). Full tilt corrections produce no significant change in either the overall mean direction or dispersion. However, application of incremental bedding tilt corrections reveals a significant (95% confidence level) improvement in grouping for both areas after 40%-50% tilt correction (Figure 3b). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: ications. REGIONAL GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Hervey Group is the local name of the LambJan Facies in the Parkes-Cowra region, New South Wales. It is a thick sequence of mainly terrestrial deposits with a maximum thickness of about 2700 m, estimated from the Parkes Syncline [Conoily, 1965]. Three subgroups are further divided according to their lithological characters: in stratigraphic order these are the Beargamil Subgroup, the Nangar Subgroup, and the Cookamidgera Subgroup. Both the basal and the top subgroups are continental facies, dominated by red measures. The middle subgroup has marine intercalations at the bottom [Williams, 1977; C. Powell and D. Crane, unpublished work, 1980], and is characterized by repetitious cycles of white quartzose sandstones, red and white sandstones with some red siltstones, and then red siltstones and shales. The Hervey Group unconformably overlies the mid-Devonian granite and other older Palaeozoic rocks in this region, while fish plates from the middle part of the sequence, e.g., the Nangar Subgroup, indicate a Late Devonian age [Conoily, 1965]. The strike of the cleavage is about 10øE, and the dip is usually greater than 60 ø . Sampling was carried out mainly in the red units, although a few samples were taken from the white-brown sandstone members in the Murga area. As often as possible, both a sun compass and a magnetic compass were employed to orient the samples, while the sun compass measurements were preferred for data analysis wherever they were available. Sampling sites were located on different limbs of folds so that a fold test [Graham, 1949; McFadden and Jones, 1981] could be applied. Although most of the samples were from noncleaved rocks, some slightly to well-cleaved samples were specifically collected from the Murga area in order to further test the time relation between the remanent magnetization and the deformation. A total of 104 samples, consisting both of short drill cores and block samples, were collected from 11 sites. Nine of the sites were either in, or just above the Famennian marine unit, and the other two just below it (Figure 1). Thus the studied rocks are believed to be latest Devonian (Famennian) in age. Results from the North China Block The Cambrian poles of the NCB are from the Maozhuang and Xuzhuang formations of Shandong and Liaoning provinces, consisting of red oolitic dolomites. THE CAMBRIAN POSITION OF THE NORTH CHINA BLOCK The suggested southern hemisphere position for the NCB might seem to be strange, so that further explanation is necessary. In the NCB there is a great sedimentary hiatus from Upper Ordovician to Lower Carboniferous. The oldest post-Cambrian pole with known polarity is the Permian pole (McElhinny et al., 1981; Lin, 1984). If we assume that the apparent polar wander was less than 90 degrees from the Cambrian to the Permian, which seems reasonable in the light of the APW paths for the other continents, then the polarity ambiguity of the Cambrian pole can be resolved. Based on this suggestion, we propose that the pole position at 15.0N, 298.6E is the 110 LIN, FULLER AND ZHANG Cambrian north pole. If this is correct, then it follows the NCB must have been in the southern himisphere in the Cambrian. If the Nicola Volcanics had been hematized before the mid-Cretaceous, then their B component would indicate a similar rotation and translation to that found for their A com- ponent and for the Guichon and Copper Mountain plutons. Correcting the B component for this rotation and translation moves its pole to an PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE TRIASSIC NICOLA VOLCANICS 241 untenable position in the Pacific Ocean off the apparent polar wander (APW) path for the North American craton (Irving, 1979). Therefore, the most likely age for the origin of the post-tilting B component is Middle Eocene, coincident with extrusion of the Princeton Group volcanics. Relative to the Eocene reference pole for the craton, this suggests that ~ 15 ° of the clockwise rotation and ~7 ° of the northward translation of Quesnellia occurred during Eocene and Oligocene time. INTRODUCTION The Upper Triassic Nicola Volcanics are the oldest extrusive rocks exposed in the Quesnellia Subterrane of allochthonous composite Terrane I (Monger et al., 1982) in southcentral British Columbia (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic studies on Lower Jurassic plutons have shown that Quesnellia has been translated northward by ,-~ 13 ° of paleolatitude and rotated clockwise by --~43 ° between Late Cretaceous and pre-Miocene time (Symons, 1973, 1983a) as part of the overall motion of Terrane I (Monger and Irving, 1980; Symons, 1983b) and of the Cordillera overall (e.g., Beck et al., 1981). GEOLOGY The Nicola Group is exposed in three north-trending belts bounded by major faults (Fig. 2). The Central Belt was deposited first and it is com- prised of subaerial and submarine andesites and basalts, breccias, con- glomerates and lahars with minor comagmatic diorite and syenite intrusions. The Eastern Belt consists of volcanic sedimentary rocks, lahars with minor basalt flows and syenite stocks. The Western Belt was deposited last and it is comprised of andesitic to rhyolitic flows and pyroclastics with interbeds of limestone, volcanic conglomerate and sandstone. If the Nicola Volcanics had been hematized before the mid-Cretaceous, then their B component would indicate a similar rotation and translation to that found for their A com- ponent and for the Guichon and Copper Mountain plutons. Correcting the B component for this rotation and translation moves its pole to an PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE TRIASSIC NICOLA VOLCANICS 241 untenable position in the Pacific Ocean off the apparent polar wander (APW) path for the North American craton (Irving, 1979). Therefore, the most likely age for the origin of the post-tilting B component is Middle Eocene, coincident with extrusion of the Princeton Group volcanics. Relative to the Eocene reference pole for the craton, this suggests that ~ 15 ° of the clockwise rotation and ~7 ° of the northward translation of Quesnellia occurred during Eocene and Oligocene time. The Triassic Nicola Volcanics are the oldest strata in the QuesneUia Subterrane of composite Terrane I which is located in the southcentral Cordillera of British Columbia. A paleomagnetic study using AF and thermal demagnetization methods of 563 speciments from 56 sites in three petrologically and tec- tonically distinct belts of the Nicola isolates two remanence components residing dominantly in hematite. The prefolding A component found after 560°C thermal cleaning gives a pole position of I1.3°W, 52.7°N (60=4.7 °, 6 m =7.2°), and appears to be caused by alteration associated with major Early Jurassic intrusive events. The dominant postfolding B component is best defined by 565°C thermal cleaning and gives a pole of 303.0°W, 82.5°N (60 = 6.6 °, 6m = 8.6°). It likely reflects alteration associated with Eocene volcanism. Combined with previous paleomagnetic data

ent is best defined by 565°C thermal cleaning and gives a pole of 303.0°W, 82.5°N (60 = 6.6 °, 6m = 8.6°). It likely reflects alteration associated with Eocene volcanism. Combined with previous paleomagnetic data, these results indicate that Quesnellia was translated northward by ~ 13 ° of paleoatitude along with the rest of Terrane I and rotated ~45 ° clockwise during Late Cretaceous to Oligocene time with ~7 ° of the translation and 15 ° of the rotation occurring during Eocene to Oligocene time. INTRODUCTION The Upper Triassic Nicola Volcanics are the oldest extrusive rocks exposed in the Quesnellia Subterrane of allochthonous composite Terrane I (Monger et al., 1982) in southcentral British Columbia (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic studies on Lower Jurassic plutons have shown that Quesnellia has been translated northward by ,-~ 13 ° of paleolatitude and rotated clockwise by --~43 ° between Late Cretaceous and pre-Miocene time (Symons, 1973, 1983a) as part of the overall motion of Terrane I (Monger and Irving, 1980; Symons, 1983b) and of the Cordillera overall (e.g., Beck et al., 1981). GEOLOGY The Nicola Group is exposed in three north-trending belts bounded by major faults (Fig. 2). The Central Belt was deposited first and it is com- prised of subaerial and submarine andesites and basalts, breccias, con- glomerates and lahars with minor comagmatic diorite and syenite intrusions. The Eastern Belt consists of volcanic sedimentary rocks, lahars with minor basalt flows and syenite stocks. The Western Belt was deposited last and it is comprised of andesitic to rhyolitic flows and pyroclastics with interbeds of limestone, volcanic conglomerate and sandstone. Paleomagnetic studies were also performed on 103 igneous rock samples taken from 19 dikes in the Arica dike swarm, which intrudes into the Atajana Formation sandstone. They showed 10°-15° counterclockwise rotation of the Arica region, northernmost Chile, with respect to the stable South American platform. These data suggest that the nor- thernmost Chilean region underwent a tectonic rotation at least after the Cretaceous period, as the southern end of the Peruvian block. 1. of the Peruvian block. 1. Introduction The recent paleomagnetic studies of the Central Andean area(PALMER et al., 1980; HEKI, 1983; HEKI et al., 1983, 1984, 1985a, b; KONG et al., 1984)are revealing that the Peruvian Andes has zotated counterclockwise as a nearly rigid "block" giving rise to the present elbow shape of the Andes at the Peru -Chile border(Bolivian orocline; CAREY, 1955). The northernmost part of Chile(the Arica region)is an area of paleomagnetic importance because it accurately cor- responds to the "hinge" of the Bolivian orocline. In this article, we discuss the Cretaceous paleomagnetic data of this region obtained from a red sandstone layer of the Atajana Formation and from a dike swarm(the Arica dike swarm)in- truding into this formation. 2. Introduction The Andean region is a subduction zone characterized by the Peru-Chile trench and the Andean orogenic belt. This subduction zone is a continental arc with no apparent marginal seas at present. Paleomagnetic studies of the Andean belt have been performed to clarify tectonic deformation. In the southernmost part of Andes in Chile the structural trend changes from north-south to northwest-southeast. This change is ascribed to a post Cretaceous deformation by the paleomagnetic method (DALZIEL et a1.,1973; BURNS et al.,1980). In the northernmost part, the trend of the Andean belt changes from northeast-southwest to east-west. MACDONALD and OPDYKE (1972) reported a shift in magnetic declination for the Cretaceous rocks which infers tectonic rotation of northernmost part of the Andean belt. From paleomagnetic and K-Ar geochronological studies PALMER et al. (1980) suggested post-Jurassic counterclockwise rotation of the A

northernmost part of the Andean belt. From paleomagnetic and K-Ar geochronological studies PALMER et al. (1980) suggested post-Jurassic counterclockwise rotation of the Arica region in Central Andes. Further HEKI et al. (1983) carried out intensive sampling and measurement of Cretaceous rocks in Peru and in northernmost Chile. They concluded that the Peruvian block rotated counterclockwise by about 30°after the Cretaceous and that this rotation is a cause of the abrupt change of trend from north-south trend in the Chilean Andes to northwest-southeast of the Peruvian. HEKI et al. (1985) also showed a slight declination shift of Neogene dike swarm in Peru. This deformation is quite interesting on account of its characteristics as an intraplate one, whereas the others in the southernmost and northernmost parts have occurred at edges of the continental 477 478 H. TSUNAKAWA et al. plate. The possible time of counterclockwise rotation of Peruvian block is, therefore, between the early Tertiary and the recent. In order to obtain constraints to determine timing of tectonic rotation of the Peruvian block we further studied paleomagnetism of Late Miocene to Early Pliocene sedimentary rocks and Latest Miocene volcanic rocks in southern Peru. 2. Introduction Secular variation is a significant characteristics of the geomagnetic field. Volcanic rocks are very useful to study paleosecular variation because of their stable thermoremanent magnetization although we obtain spot-reading data. Outcrops of many independent lavas are relatively easy to be found at hotspot areas such as oceanic islands but not in other regions. On the other hand a dike swarm usually occurs in volcanic regions as more than one hundred intrusions of subterranean volcanism. Its activity duration is regarded to be in the order of 105 years similar to that of a stratovolcano (NAKAMURA, 1977). A dike swarm, therefore, probably records paleosecular variation of the geomagnetic field during the time span sufficient to reflect its nature. From this viewpoint we performed a paleomagnetic study on the Ashitaka dike swarm in the southern part of Central Japan and report its result in this paper. 2. However these rocks are covered by the Ashitaka loam, which is identified with the Kanto loam supplied by the Fuji and Hakone volcanoes. Magnetic components are present when a specimen, sample or site contains multiple magnetization with a different direction and origin. Four components of magnetization (A, B, C and D) were isolated (Fig. 3). The principle of grouping and identification of the components is the following. Magnetic components are present when a specimen, sample or site contains multiple magnetization with a different direction and origin. Introduction Recent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that

ent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that Southwest Japan suffered a clockwise rotation at about 15 Ma. The timing of the rotation is much later than previously assumed (KAWAI et al., 1971), and the duration of the rotation seems extremely short. Current research is directed toward increasing the number of paleomagnetic data near the timing of the rotation. This is important for more detailed description of the rotational process, which has a significance in reconstruction of tectonic history around Southwest Japan. Paleomagnetic measurements have been made on samples from the Morozaki Group and the Mizunami Group, typical sequences of the Setouchi Miocene Series sporadically extending in Southwest Japan (Fig. 1). Among them, the late Early Miocene Ichishi Group was shown to have remanent magnetization having easterly deflected declinations (HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984). The age of the Ichishi Group, about 16 Ma, gives a critical timing for the beginning of the rotation of Southwest Japan. While the Morozaki and Mizunami Groups are correlative to the Ichishi Group in part, the upper members of both groups are suggested to be younger than the Ichishi Group. Introduction Recent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that

ent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that Southwest Japan suffered a clockwise rotation at about 15 Ma. The timing of the rotation is much later than previously assumed (KAWAI et al., 1971), and the duration of the rotation seems extremely short. Current research is directed toward increasing the number of paleomagnetic data near the timing of the rotation. This is important for more detailed description of the rotational process, which has a significance in reconstruction of tectonic history around Southwest Japan. Paleomagnetic measurements have been made on samples from the Morozaki Group and the Mizunami Group, typical sequences of the Setouchi Miocene Series sporadically extending in Southwest Japan (Fig. 1). Among them, the late Early Miocene Ichishi Group was shown to have remanent magnetization having easterly deflected declinations (HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984). The age of the Ichishi Group, about 16 Ma, gives a critical timing for the beginning of the rotation of Southwest Japan. While the Morozaki and Mizunami Groups are correlative to the Ichishi Group in part, the upper members of both groups are suggested to be younger than the Ichishi Group. 6 Timing of Rotational Motion of Southwest Japan Inferred from Paleomagnetism of the Setouchi Miocene Series Akira HAYASHIDA Laboratory of Earth Science, Doshisha University, Kyoto, Japan (Received January 14, 1986) Paleomagnetic measurements have been made on tuff and mud samples from 25 sites of the Morozaki Group and the Mizunami Group, distributed in the eastern part of Southwest Japan. Stability tests by alternating field and thermal demagnetization reveal the existence of characteristic remanent magnetization, of which directions show significant clockwise deflection; the mean declination shift exceeds 50° in the late Early Miocene members (N6-N8), and is less than 30° in the early Middle Miocene members (N9). This result, compared with the other paleomagnetic data from the Setouchi Miocene Series and the volcanic rocks in the San'in district, suggests that coherent rotation of Southwest Japan began between the late Early Miocene and the early Middle Miocene. Nearly a half of the rotation might have been attained in the stage of Zone N9, which possibly corresponds to the period of the opening and increasing subsidence in the Japan Sea. 1. Introduction Recent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that

ent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that Southwest Japan suffered a clockwise rotation at about 15 Ma. The timing of the rotation is much later than previously assumed (KAWAI et al., 1971), and the duration of the rotation seems extremely short. Current research is directed toward increasing the number of paleomagnetic data near the timing of the rotation. This is important for more detailed description of the rotational process, which has a significance in reconstruction of tectonic history around Southwest Japan. Paleomagnetic measurements have been made on samples from the Morozaki Group and the Mizunami Group, typical sequences of the Setouchi Miocene Series sporadically extending in Southwest Japan (Fig. 1). Among them, the late Early Miocene Ichishi Group was shown to have remanent magnetization having easterly deflected declinations (HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984). The age of the Ichishi Group, about 16 Ma, gives a critical timing for the beginning of the rotation of Southwest Japan. While the Morozaki and Mizunami Groups are correlative to the Ichishi Group in part, the upper members of both groups are suggested to be younger than the Ichishi Group. section_candidates.excerpt: A and MATSUDA (1985) gave one explanation that the cusp was formed by collisions of the Tanzawa and the Izu Block on the basis of the exotic origin of the Tanzawa Block and the past plate motion. In the Kanto Mountains located on the east wing of the cusp structure, paleomagnetic studies have been scarcely attempted heretofore. The Chichibu Tertiary System, exposed in the central part of the Kanto Mountains, consists of early Miocene marine sediments (Fig. 1). Defining the paleomagnetic direction in this area will give us a better understanding of the relationship between the rotation of Southwest Japan (OTOFUJI et al., 1985) and the formation of the cusp structure. In this paper, we describe the paleomagnetism on the early Miocene marine sediments of the Chichibu Basin and discuss a tectonic process to form the cusp of zonal structure in Central Japan. 2. Geologic Setting The geologic map of the Chichibu Basin is shown in Fig. 2. The Basin extends about 15km in an east-west direction and nearly 12km in a north-south direction, and is filled with early Miocene marine sediments with a thickness of more than 6000 m. The marine sedimentary basin is surrounded on all sides by pre-Tertiary rocks 335 336 H. HYODO and N. NIITsuMA Fig. 1. Index map of the studied area (shaded rect

The marine strata are homoclinally dipping southeastward, while at the southeastern part of the basin the strata are irregularly folded. Introduction During the last few years paleomagnetic studies have been intensively made on Cenozoic rocks in the Japanese Islands. Tectonic movements of the islands have been discussed based on their results. Major paleomagnetic results of these works were recently reviewed by ToSHA and KoNo (1985) and HIROOKA (1983). eviewed by ToSHA and KoNo (1985) and HIROOKA (1983). Topics on Cenozoic time are summarized as follows: the directions of the natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) in pre-Miocene rocks were systematically different from those at present in northeast (NE) and southwest (SW) Honshu Islands. Therefore it is inferred that NE and SW Honshu Islands have undergone counterclockwise and clockwise rotation, respectively (e.g., OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; OTOFUJI et al., 1985; TOSHA and HAMANO, 1986). The analysis of paleo-stress field is one of the most useful methods to discuss the tectonics, which is derived from the directions of strikes in dike swarms and faults and those of veins in ore deposits. Besides as a stress indicator most of the dikes are composed of igneous rocks and their remanent magnetizations are usually intensive and less disturbable by some late tectonic processes. Hence, dikes are also useful for paleomagnetic works. Introduction The Korean Peninsula is situated between North China platform and trench- island arc-back arc basin systems of Japan and Ryukyu. The former behaves as a stable craton subjected to only epeirogenic movements for over a thousand million years. The latter is one of the most active areas at present on the earth; while new igneous products are added and allochthonous terrains are accreted on the island arc, older geological phenomena have been obscured. In the peculiar situation of the Korean Peninsula, the igneous and sedimentary rocks have been fairly continuously produced from Archaeozoic age to Quaternary, and they have been preserved on the peninsula (UM and REEDMAN, 1975). The Korean Peninsula is, therefore, a rare area where the apparent polar wandering path (APWP) can be expected to be traced back to 2700 Ma. Our ultimate objective is to obtain the paleomagnetic direction change during 2700 Ma from the Korean Peninsula. Introduction The Korean Peninsula is situated between North China platform and trench- island arc-back arc basin systems of Japan and Ryukyu. The former behaves as a stable craton subjected to only epeirogenic movements for over a thousand million years. The latter is one of the most active areas at present on the earth; while new igneous products are added and allochthonous terrains are accreted on the island arc, older geological phenomena have been obscured. In the peculiar situation of the Korean Peninsula, the igneous and sedimentary rocks have been fairly continuously produced from Archaeozoic age to Quaternary, and they have been preserved on the peninsula (UM and REEDMAN, 1975). The Korean Peninsula is, therefore, a rare area where the apparent polar wandering path (APWP) can be expected to be traced back to 2700 Ma. Our ultimate objective is to obtain the paleomagnetic direction change during 2700 Ma from the Korean Peninsula. The aim of the present work is to estimate the paleomagnetic direction for the period between Permian and Cretaceous. †Present address: Earthquake Research Institute, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan. 387 388 Y. Introduction The Korean Peninsula is situated between North China platform and trench- island arc-back arc basin systems of Japan and Ryukyu. The former behaves as a stable craton subjected to only epeirogenic movements for over a thousand million years. The latter is one of the most active areas at present on the earth; while new igneous products are added and allochthonous terrains are accreted on the island arc, older geological phenomena have been obscured. In the peculiar situation of the Korean Peninsula, the igneous and sedimentary rocks have been fairly continuously produced from Archaeozoic age to Quaternary, and they have been preserved on the peninsula (UM and REEDMAN, 1975). The Korean Peninsula is, therefore, a rare area where the apparent polar wandering path (APWP) can be expected to be traced back to 2700 Ma. Our ultimate objective is to obtain the paleomagnetic direction change during 2700 Ma from the Korean Peninsula. The aim of the present work is to estimate the paleomagnetic direction for the period between Permian and Cretaceous. †Present address: Earthquake Research Institute, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan. 387 388 Y. Introduction The Korean Peninsula is situated between North China platform and trench- island arc-back arc basin systems of Japan and Ryukyu. The former behaves as a stable craton subjected to only epeirogenic movements for over a thousand million years. The latter is one of the most active areas at present on the earth; while new igneous products are added and allochthonous terrains are accreted on the island arc, older geological phenomena have been obscured. In the peculiar situation of the Korean Peninsula, the igneous and sedimentary rocks have been fairly continuously produced from Archaeozoic age to Quaternary, and they have been preserved on the peninsula (UM and REEDMAN, 1975). The Korean Peninsula is, therefore, a rare area where the apparent polar wandering path (APWP) can be expected to be traced back to 2700 Ma. Our ultimate objective is to obtain the paleomagnetic direction change during 2700 Ma from the Korean Peninsula. Fourty five examples at 13 sites were collected from Permian strata, 44 samples at 10 sites were from Triassic ones, 91 samples at 23 sites were from Jurassic ones, and 290 samples at 65 sites were from Cretaceous. Two or more specimens 25mm in diameter and 25mm long were prepared from each sample in the laboratory. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured with a two component SCT cryogenic magnetometer. The stability of remanent magnetization was investi- gated through progressive demagnetization treatment by both thermal and alternat- ing field (AF) methods. The progressive AF demagnetization was made with a magnetically shielded three axis tumbler and thermal one was with a non-inductively wound electric furnace enclosed in a cylindrical mu-metal shield. One specimen in each site was cleaned as a pilot specimen in a stepwise progression with alternating peak field ranging from 5mT to 50mT. The Gyeongsang Supergroup (Cretaceous) The Gyeongsang Supergroup is a major unconformity-bounded unit of non- marine sedimentary and igneous rocks of about the whole span of the Cretaceous System. The Gyeongsang Supergroup is divided into three groups (CHANG, 1975): The Sindong, Hayan and Yuchon Groups in ascending order. The Singdong Group consists of sediments of prevolcanic phase, the Hayan Group comprises nonvolcanic sediments with some volcanic horizons, and Yuchon Group consists of volcanic formation. (1985) compiled these results, and discussed the process of tectonic rotation of Southwest Japan. According to them the mean declination of the rocks older than 15.5Ma is approximately 47°E, while that of the rocks younger than 14.5Ma shows no significant offset from the present dipole field. They concluded that Southwest Japan was rotated clockwise through 47° within a period from 15.5Ma to 14.5Ma in association with the opening of the Sea of Japan. This paper describes the paleomagnetic results obtained from Miocene rocks distributed in Fukui Prefecture, the northeastern part (the Hokuriku district) of Southwest Japan, and discusses the tectonic rotation of this area. This area was geologically mapped in detail, and its stratigraphic relations were well established by TSUKANO and MIURA (1954), MIURA (1979), and NAKAGAWA et al. (1985). Furthermore, chronological studies using fission-track method (HIROOKA et al., 1972; NAKAJIMA et al., 1983; NAKAJIMA and MIZUSHIMA, 1984; NAKAJIMA et al., 1985), which yielded ten radiometric ages ranging from 27Ma to 11Ma, clarified the history of igneous activity in this area. (1985) compiled these results, and discussed the process of tectonic rotation of Southwest Japan. According to them the mean declination of the rocks older than 15.5Ma is approximately 47°E, while that of the rocks younger than 14.5Ma shows no significant offset from the present dipole field. They concluded that Southwest Japan was rotated clockwise through 47° within a period from 15.5Ma to 14.5Ma in association with the opening of the Sea of Japan. This paper describes the paleomagnetic results obtained from Miocene rocks distributed in Fukui Prefecture, the northeastern part (the Hokuriku district) of Southwest Japan, and discusses the tectonic rotation of this area. This area was geologically mapped in detail, and its stratigraphic relations were well established by TSUKANO and MIURA (1954), MIURA (1979), and NAKAGAWA et al. (1985). Furthermore, chronological studies using fission-track method (HIROOKA et al., 1972; NAKAJIMA et al., 1983; NAKAJIMA and MIZUSHIMA, 1984; NAKAJIMA et al., 1985), which yielded ten radiometric ages ranging from 27Ma to 11Ma, clarified the history of igneous activity in this area. The metavolcanic rocks are massive or pillowed (mainly) lavas of andesitic and mostly basaltic composition and the dyke swarms are composed of basaltic and doleritic diabases; both lithological groups are metamorphosed to the sub- greenschist (pumpellyite) facies. Pyroclastics, tuffs and volcanic agglomerates are also present in minor quantities. The NRM intensities of the metalavas and diabases are very weak. Mag- netic, titanomagnetite and occasional grains of hematite are the magnetic memory carriers. Native iron was also detected in minute quantities. In order to obtain some pertinent information relative to the stability of the NRM component, stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization was con- ducted on 300 of the specimens in the 50-800 Oersteds range and the others were demagnetized at an optimum AF intensity. Approximately 1000 of the specimens underwent thermal treatment in the 100-550C range; thermal de- magnetization was judged less efficient than AF demagnetization and for this reason, the remaining specimens were all AF demagnetized. The limestones magnetized after iithification and incorporation as clasts into a Middle Ordovician breccia. Hence, the limestones do not carry a detrital or other primary remanence despite their very low conodont colour alteration index of 1. It also accords with pole positions obtained from Chinese, Siberian and European Cretaceous rocks. From the paleomagnetic data for the granites and volcanic rocks of the Cretaceous, it is concluded that the South Korean land mass has not been subjected to sufficient local tectonic movements to generate a change in the direction of primary magnetic vectors of the granites or of the volcanic rocks since the Cretaceous. Soper SUMMARY: The well known coastal flexure of central E Greenland, with its associated dyke swarm, affects a thick pile of Tertiary basalts and the underlying basement gneisses. It is a major tectonic/magmatic feature of this 'trailing edge' type continental margin. The original interpretation of Wager & Deer (1938) envisaged the emplacement of the dykes as a fan-shaped swarm in the convex arc of the flexure. Nielsen (1975, 1978) recognized several episodes of dyke emplacement. He interpreted the main swarm (THOL 1) as earlier than the flexure, emplaced vertically into the horizontal basalt pile and subsequently tilted by antithetic faulting during the formation of the flexure. A palaeomagnetic study of the THOL 1 and later dykes shows that the former were emplaced in their present inclined attitude. This discriminates in favour of Wager's interpretation, while remaining consistent with Nielsen's view of the post-flexural magmatic history. Modifications to Nielsen's scheme are suggested to conform with the new evidence, and the implications in relation to the mechanism of flexuring, the timing o

nterpretation, while remaining consistent with Nielsen's view of the post-flexural magmatic history. Modifications to Nielsen's scheme are suggested to conform with the new evidence, and the implications in relation to the mechanism of flexuring, the timing of tholeiitic magmatism, and the relationship of both to the early spreading history of this sector of the NE Atlantic, are discussed. The coastal flexure in E Greenland is a seaward facing monocline which marks the present coastline for some 600 km between approximately 66 and 70"N (Fig. 1). To the NE of Kangerdlugssuaq, along the Blosseville Kyst, the flexure affects Palaeogene basalts. On the outer headlands for 75 km as far as Jensen Fjord, seaward dips of 35-55" are observed and the mono- cline is associated with an intense swarm of basic dykes which dip landward, roughly normal to the flows. Further NE the coast recedes. Dips are shallow and the dyke swarm less intense; the flexure apparently lies offshore. Towards the northern end of the Blos- Seville Kyst seaward dips of up to 30" again occur but these are in part due to block faulting and the flexure is weak. section_candidates.excerpt: ll known coastal flexure of central E Greenland, with its associated dyke swarm, affects a thick pile of Tertiary basalts and the underlying basement gneisses. It is a major tectonic/magmatic feature of this 'trailing edge' type continental margin. The original interpretation of Wager & Deer (1938) envisaged the emplacement of the dykes as a fan-shaped swarm in the convex arc of the flexure. Nielsen (1975, 1978) recognized several episodes of dyke emplacement. He interpreted the main swarm (THOL 1) as earlier than the flexure, emplaced vertically into the horizontal basalt pile and subsequently tilted by antithetic faulting during the formation of the flexure. A palaeomagnetic study of the THOL 1 and later dykes shows that the former were emplaced in their present inclined attitude. This discriminates in favour of Wager's interpretation, while remaining consistent with Nielsen's view of the post-flexural magmatic history. Modifications to Nielsen's scheme are suggested to conform with the new evidence, and the implications in relation to the mechanism of flexuring, the timing of tholeiitic magmatism, and the relationship of both to the early spreading history of this sector of the NE Atlantic, are discussed. The coastal flexure in E Greenland is a seaward facing monocline which marks the present coastline for some 600 km between approximately 66 and 70"N (Fig. 1). To the NE of Kangerdlugssuaq, along the Blosseville Kyst, the flexure affects Palaeogene basalts. On the outer headlands for 75 km as far as Jensen Fjord, seaward dips of 35-55" are observed and the mono- cline is associated with an intense swarm of basic dykes which dip landward, roughly normal to the flows. Further NE the coast recedes. Dips are shallow and the dyke swarm less intense; the flexure apparently lies offshore. Towards the northern end of the Blos- Seville Kyst seaward dips of up to 30" again occur but these are in part due to block faulting and the flexure is weak. To the SE of Kangerdlugssuaq, at a deeper erosional level, the course of the flexure is marked in the basement gneiss complex by en echelon zones of intense dyke injection (Bridgwater et al. 1978). uter headlands for 75 km as far as Jensen Fjord, seaward dips of 35-55" are observed and the mono- cline is associated with an intense swarm of basic dykes which dip landward, roughly normal to the flows. Further NE the coast recedes. Dips are shallow and the dyke swarm less intense; the flexure apparently lies offshore. Towards the northern end of the Blos- Seville Kyst seaward dips of up to 30" again occur but these are in part due to block faulting and the flexure is weak. To the SE of Kangerdlugssuaq, at a deeper erosional level, the course of the flexure is marked in the basement gneiss complex by en echelon zones of intense dyke injection (Bridgwater et al. 1978). The dykes dip landward and, where patches of extrusive basalt are preserved, are again normal to the flows. Since their discovery (Wager & Deer 1938; Wager 1947) the dyke swarm and flexure have come to be regarded as a classic example of extensional-type magma tectonics on a continental margin. Wager's interpretation of the structure presaged modern ideas on the association of vertical displacements with changes in crustal thickness and thermal conditions in the mantle. He viewed the dykes as a fan-shaped swarm emplaced in the antiformal (convex) part of the monocline due to outer-arc extension

Duff SUMMARY: Scattered, but stable NRM (natural remanent magnetization) in the Jersey diorite-metagabbro complex, probably acquired during the formation of the complex, can be ascribed to 2 main geological processes: (i) stoping of the late Precambrian or early Cambrian diorites and metagabbros by the Jersey granites, which caused pre-stoping NRM to be dispersed by block rotation and subsidence in the granite melt; this was the largest contributor to palaeomagnetic.matter; (ii) hybridization of the parent gabbro during granite intrusion, which added a dioritic generation of magnetite and its NRM to the NRM carried by the gabbro, and probably also caused variable, partial remagnetization of the gabbroic NRM before stoping. Palaeomagnetic results suggest that the complex NRM of the Jersey diorite-metagabbro complex was not acquired as a VRM (viscous remanent magnetization) in a recent geomagnetic field. Rather, the explanation of the unusual scatter of stable NRM directions in these rocks is probably to be sought in the well- documented sequence of geological events that gov- erned the formation of the diorite-metagabbro com- plex (Wells & Wooldridge 1931; Bishop 1954; Wells & Bishop 1955; Key 1974). Origin of the within-block scatter Microprobe and optical results (Duff 1978) strongly suggest that the within-block scatter of NRM direc- tions and related variable demagnetization trends (Figs 2 & 3) reflect the highly variable overprinting of an original gabbroic NRM during hybridization of the gabbro (dioritization) by the Jersey granites. The re- sulting multicomponent NRM may have originated in either or both of the following ways: (i) variable partial remagnetization of primary gabbroic NRM; (ii) acquisition by magnetites grown during dioritization of a dioritic NRM in addition to that already present in the primary gabbroic titanomagnetites. Typically, the original gabbroic assemblage has been altered to a dioritic assemblage at temperatures of the upper amphibolite or granulite facies (Key 1974). At these temperatures (>500" C) only a small amount of the original remanence may survive in grains with high blocking temperatures (Pullaiah et al. 1975), so it is likely that the original gabbro was entirely or partially remagnetized during hybridization by the granite melt. The metagabbroic mineral as- semblage of the NW diorite suggests that it has been little altered from the parent gabbro (Key 1974). Accordingly, the steeper direction of the NW diorite NRM probably reflects an older magnetization than in most of the SE diorite blocks. The association of different mean NRM directions with small, separately stoped diorite blocks within a single sampling site in SE Jersey strongly supports scattering of an NRM acquired before stoping by block rotation and subsidence. Badham SUMMARY: The Lizard Complex of SW England has recently been interpreted as representing a fragment of oceanic lithosphere that was thrust on to the continental crust of S Cornwall in the Devonian as a result of tectonic processes at a convergent plate margin. A palaeomagnetic study has been carried out on the ultramafics. gabbros and dykes of the E coast section to examine possible tectonic movements that might have been associated with this history of formation. A component of stable magnetization having a shallow to intermediate negative inclination and a SSW declination has been identified in each of these lithologies. This direction is similar to the Permian geomagnetic field direction for SW England, and one interpretation of the results is that the Lizard rocks were remagnetized in the early Permian, perhaps as a result of heating associated with emplacement of the Variscan batholiths. However. no mineralogical or other evidence for widespread heating of the Lizard Complex in the Permian has yet been identified. The Barnes High Sandstone and the Perna Bed were hand-sampled and 25 mm cores were drilled from the hand samples in the laboratory. In the Shepherd's Chine Section 48 samples were taken from 23 stratigraphic levels and in the Yaverland section 70 samples from 31 levels. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the specimens was measured with a Molspin spinner magneto- meter based on the design described by Molyneux (1971). To check the reliability of the determinations triplicate measurements of the magnetization were carried out regularly and the 95% confidence limit (ag5) of the mean direction was calculated (Fisher 1953). Ater a time span of 2-6 weeks the NRM was re-measured to check on the possible acquistion of components of viscous remanent magnetization in the laboratory. Two specimens from each sampling level were then subjected to stepwise alternating field (a.f.) demagnetization in peak applied fields up to 35 milliTesla (mT) using increments of 5mT. This magnetozone has a thickness of some 15 m and its upper boundary is well defined in the Yaverland section but is obscured in the Shepherd's Chine Section due to cliff slumping. The lower boundary is well established in both sections and lies some 15 m above the Barnes High Sandstone Member in the Shepherd's Chine section and 12m above this unit at Yaverland. This boundary provides a useful chron-stratigraphic datum. A comparison with established geomagnetic polarity timescales for the Cretaceous indicates that the Vectis magnetozone may be correlated either with Lower Aptian reverse polarity Chron CM-0 or with Lower Barremian Chron CM-l, with the former being the more likely. An important implication of this interpretation is that the base of the Aptian stage, as defined from Tethyan foraminiferal zones, must lie within the Vectis Formation, at least 25-30m beneath the top of the Shepherd's Chine Member, rather than at the top of this member as hitherto commonly accepted. ORS) is the largest of the Devonian massifs in Norway (Fig. l), and comprises c. 25 km of mainly axially-deposited alluvial grey sandstones and siltstones interfingering with marginal fan- conglomerates (Steel et al. 1985). Plant and fish fossils found in the upper part of the succession indicate an upper Lower Devonian age. The great apparent stratigraphical thickness, alluvial sedimentation and basin asymmetry, together with repetitions of basin-wide, upward-coarsening sequences associated with lateral extension, were among the factors that led Bryhni (1964, 1978) and Steel and co-workers (see review in Steel et al. 1985) to the conclusion that the Hornelen ‘Basin’ was tectonically generated. The basin developed with a principal component of hinge-faulting or dextral oblique shear along, or close to, the present northern marginal fault (Figs lb & 2). Depocentres were considered to have migrated eastwards with time, in an opposite direction to the palaeoflow indicators. Over much of the outcrop of the Devonian sediments there are few penetrative effects of deformation. The rocks abound in sedimentary structures, and primary features, such as bedding, dominate the outcrop pattern. ORS) is the largest of the Devonian massifs in Norway (Fig. l), and comprises c. 25 km of mainly axially-deposited alluvial grey sandstones and siltstones interfingering with marginal fan- conglomerates (Steel et al. 1985). Plant and fish fossils found in the upper part of the succession indicate an upper Lower Devonian age. The great apparent stratigraphical thickness, alluvial sedimentation and basin asymmetry, together with repetitions of basin-wide, upward-coarsening sequences associated with lateral extension, were among the factors that led Bryhni (1964, 1978) and Steel and co-workers (see review in Steel et al. 1985) to the conclusion that the Hornelen ‘Basin’ was tectonically generated. The basin developed with a principal component of hinge-faulting or dextral oblique shear along, or close to, the present northern marginal fault (Figs lb & 2). Depocentres were considered to have migrated eastwards with time, in an opposite direction to the palaeoflow indicators. Over much of the outcrop of the Devonian sediments there are few penetrative effects of deformation. The rocks abound in sedimentary structures, and primary features, such as bedding, dominate the outcrop pattern. Detailed sampling within the Late Permian- Middle Triassic Narrabeen Group has been carried out north and south of Sydney at coastal outcrops between Wybung Head and Coal Cliff (Fig. 1). The beds are essentially flat lying, regional dips of 1 to 2 probably being the result of Tertiary warping. The lower units of the Narrabeen Group in the coastal section north of Sydney are characterised by conglomerates and coarse grey, green, and buff coloured sandstones. The sediments were carried by streams and deposited in channels located between flood plain fine sands and thin bands of red claystone formed in part by overbank deposition. Higher in the section a relatively persistent red claystone horizon is encountered; in the northern coastal section this is known as the Patonga Claystone and a similar horizon (though possibly younger) south of Sydney is the Bald Hill Claystone (HERBERT, 1970). 2. Geology and Sampling A 25-km coastal strip of largely volcanic rocks west of Tramore, County Waterford, forms part of a wider belt of Cambrian to Silurian volcanism in south-eastern Ireland which peaked in the Upper Ordovician. The rocks are largely submarine and are considered (PHILLIPS et a1.,1976; STILLMAN, 1978; STILLMAN and WILLIAMS, 1978) to have been erupted at a continental plate margin related to a SE-dipping subduction zone and developing arc-trench system that formed part of a Lower Paleozoic Proto-Atlantic ocean; such a subduction system was postulated earlier for the Lake District and Wales (FITTON and HUGHES, 1970). STILLMAN et al. (1974), SCHIENER (1974), and STILLMAN (1978) have described the geology west of Tramore, where the volcanism is believed to have begun in Llandeilo time or somewhat earlier and was interrupted by deposition of the Tramore limestone, a fossil marker horizon of Llandeilo age (CARLISLE, 1979). The volcanism in this area ended in the Lower Caradoc (CARLISLE, 1979) and the rocks were deformed during the Caledonian orogeny. The volcanic rocks of the Waterford/Tramore region are, in decreasing order of abundance, rhyolite, basalt, andesite and dacite, the acidic rocks being predominantly pyroclastic or intrusive (STILLMAN and WILLIAMS, 1978). Alteration seems to be due mainly to weathering during or shortly after emplacement, or hydrothermal metasomism; rocks affected by a superimposed burial metamorphism commonly are of lower than greenshist facies grade (STILLMAN and WILLIAMS, 1978). GOLEBY north-south trending tectonic provinces, two of which are the Molong High and Cowra Trough (Fig. 2). The Molong High is dominantly Ordovician, with localized areas of Silurian and Devonian. The Ordovician sequences represent three episodes of tectonic activity: initial andesitic volcanism during the Early Ordovician, followed by a quiet period enabling the deposition of limestones, siltstones, and arenites during the Middle-Late Ordovician. This was followed by a further period of volcanic activity resulting in volcanic tuffs and lavas. Samples were collected stratigraphically through this sequence, and where possible, in the overlying Siluro-Devonian. The Cowra Trough (Fig. 2) formed as a result of internal rifting within the Molong High during the Late Ordovician (SCHEIBNER, 1973). It is dominantly Silurian in age, with isolated areas extending into the Middle Devonian. GOLEBY north-south trending tectonic provinces, two of which are the Molong High and Cowra Trough (Fig. 2). The Molong High is dominantly Ordovician, with localized areas of Silurian and Devonian. The Ordovician sequences represent three episodes of tectonic activity: initial andesitic volcanism during the Early Ordovician, followed by a quiet period enabling the deposition of limestones, siltstones, and arenites during the Middle-Late Ordovician. This was followed by a further period of volcanic activity resulting in volcanic tuffs and lavas. Samples were collected stratigraphically through this sequence, and where possible, in the overlying Siluro-Devonian. The Cowra Trough (Fig. 2) formed as a result of internal rifting within the Molong High during the Late Ordovician (SCHEIBNER, 1973). It is dominantly Silurian in age, with isolated areas extending into the Middle Devonian. GOLEBY north-south trending tectonic provinces, two of which are the Molong High and Cowra Trough (Fig. 2). The Molong High is dominantly Ordovician, with localized areas of Silurian and Devonian. The Ordovician sequences represent three episodes of tectonic activity: initial andesitic volcanism during the Early Ordovician, followed by a quiet period enabling the deposition of limestones, siltstones, and arenites during the Middle-Late Ordovician. This was followed by a further period of volcanic activity resulting in volcanic tuffs and lavas. Samples were collected stratigraphically through this sequence, and where possible, in the overlying Siluro-Devonian. The Cowra Trough (Fig. 2) formed as a result of internal rifting within the Molong High during the Late Ordovician (SCHEIBNER, 1973). It is dominantly Silurian in age, with isolated areas extending into the Middle Devonian. GoLEBY Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, Canberra A.C.T., Australia (Received February 25, 1980 ; Revised April 30, 1980) The palaeomagnetism of 22 formations from the Cowra Trough and Molong High of South East Australia have been studied. Samples of Ordovician through Middle Devonian age were collected in three major areas, covering a time period crucial to the understanding of the Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path of Australia. Five magnetic components have been identified: 1) A recent field overprint, 2) a secondary component related to the break up of Australia and Antarctica, 3) a predominent Devonian secondary overprint associated with the major orogenic episode, 4) a weak Silurian overprint associated with an earlier orogenic episode, and 5) primary magnetic components ranging in age from the Ordovician to the Devonian. The directions obtained enable construction of a well defined polar wander path for South East Australia and Australia as a whole. 1. GoLEBY Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, Canberra A.C.T., Australia (Received February 25, 1980 ; Revised April 30, 1980) The palaeomagnetism of 22 formations from the Cowra Trough and Molong High of South East Australia have been studied. Samples of Ordovician through Middle Devonian age were collected in three major areas, covering a time period crucial to the understanding of the Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path of Australia. Five magnetic components have been identified: 1) A recent field overprint, 2) a secondary component related to the break up of Australia and Antarctica, 3) a predominent Devonian secondary overprint associated with the major orogenic episode, 4) a weak Silurian overprint associated with an earlier orogenic episode, and 5) primary magnetic components ranging in age from the Ordovician to the Devonian. The directions obtained enable construction of a well defined polar wander path for South East Australia and Australia as a whole. 1. (1974) proposed a two plate tectonic model based on a difference of 90 degrees in the apparent pole path for the South Eastern part of the Tasman Geosyncline (as defined by PACKHAM, 1969) compared with the simplest interpretation of the pole path for the stable central Australian craton (Fig. 1A). Poles SV, MP, AV, and BG represent the Siluro-Devonian track of South East Australian sub-plate. Since the Late Devonian, the sub-plate was welded to the main craton producing a common track for the whole of Australia. Two strong points are in favour, l) all the reliable Australian poles are used, and fit stratigraphically in sequence. 2) The angular distance between the Ordovician and the Silurian sections requires less than 90 degrees movement. WILLIAMS Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara, California 93106 Paleomagnetic results from Miocene flows from the Truk Islands reveal stable magnetization having a declination of +2° and an inclina- tion of +6°, with an ci of 6.8 and a k of 45.4. This is different from the 95 present dipole field at the 95% confidence level. Ten sites are included in the analysis so that major departures from the true mean field direction due to secular variation should have been eliminated. e true mean field direction due to secular variation should have been eliminated. The result gives an ancient latitude of 3°N with a ±3° confidence interval, which is consis- tent with proposed rotation about the Hawaiian hot spot pole at a rate of 1.3 /10 years for the past 10 million years. The directions of magnet- 0 6 ization of flows of Eocene and Miocene age from Saipan reveal a mean direction of magnetization rotated clockwise from the present field direc- tion. Although there are fewer results available from Saipan than from Truk, the results appear to be recording some tectonic rotation and not simply secular variation. The Marianas limestone of Pleistocene age has a direction of magnetization concordant with the present field. These re- sults from Truk and Saipan reveal that tectonic models can indeed be tested in island arc and oceanic island environments by paleomagnetic observations. It is also clear that the paleomagnetism of such islands suf- fers from inadequate numbers of available sites and difficulties in estab- lishing tectonic control. The similarity of the rotation observed at Saipan and Guam strongly suggests that tectonic models of the Marianas must account for major rotation of the southern end of the Marianas since their formation. The model invokes the combined action of the northwestward motion of the Philippine Sea Plate and the pinning of the northern Philippines a t its southern margin by collision with the Calamian continental fragment. Member 4 consists of gray and pale gray argillaceous-laminated limestones, bioclastic limestones, and oolitic limestones. Member 5 is composed of purplish red calcareous mudstones with intercalated argillaceous limestones. Conformably overlying these units are the Lower Triassic Maocaopu Formation and the Middle Triassic Songzikan Formation, both consisting mainly of dolomites and limestones deposited in a marine environment, which are in turn, disconformably overlain by Upper Triassic quartzose sandstones, shales, and siltstones with coal seams (Xujiahe Formation). The Lower Triassic sediments vary lithologically on a regional basis, from west to east, changing from a proximal clastic facies (Feixiaguan Formation) through a mixed facies of clastics and carbonates (Yelang Formation) to a carbonate marine facies (Daye Formation) (Yang Zunyi et al., 1982). The sampling area is in the transitional facies zone of mixed clastics and limestone. For this reason the Yelang Formation at the northwest limb is thicker and with more clastic beds. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: ades, New York Abstract. Two widely separated localities have been sampled from Triassic Formations of the Yangtze platforms. The first is from the border area between Sichuan and Guizhou provinces, where the Early Triassic Yelang Formation was sampled at 15 sites, located on both flanks of an anticline. Characteristic high-temperature components were isolated from nine sites, the remainder were severely overprinted by a recent field. Two polarities are present, one directed toward the northeast with shallow positive inclinations, and the other to the southwest with almost horizontal inclinations. The northeast group passes the fold test at the 95% level. The second area of study was from the city of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, where 19 sites were drilled from three formations ranging in age from the lower to upper Triassic. The samples are severely overprinted with a component that is almost vertical and whose origin is unclear. However, in 23 of the samples, a high-temperature component was isolated directed to the northeast and positive and to the southwest and negative. The fold test is indeterminate. The most prominent of these are now known as the Sino-Korea platform, the Yangtze platform, and the most recent addition, the Indian subcontinent. One of the most important means of studying the tectonic history of these paleopiates is through the determination of paleomagnetic pole positions through time. Such studies yield information on paleolatitudes of the different blocks and provide important constraints concerning the times of accretion of the different blocks (Irving, 1979). Recent tectonic synthesis in the region has lead to widely differing interpretations of the geological history of the region. Klimetz (1983) believes that the South China block accreted to Eurasia in post-Triassic times, while Zhang et al. (1984) and Mattauer et al. (1985) believe that the North and South China blocks were joined in the Devonian or earlier times.
